paragraphs: This paper investigates which parts of a convolutional LSTM actually help recognize gestures. It starts from architectures that combine a three-dimensional convolutional network with a ConvLSTM, then changes individual components to examine how spatial information and information across time are combined.

The evaluated variants remove convolutions from the three gates, apply attention to the incoming features, or rebuild the input and output gates using modified channel-wise attention. These comparisons probe whether the gates need spatial processing and whether attention inside them improves feature fusion. In the reported evaluations, gate convolutions contribute little, and attention in the input and output gates does not improve fusion.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that, when spatial or spatiotemporal features are already supplied, ConvLSTM mainly contributes by combining information across recurrent steps. They consequently derive an LSTM variant that retains convolutions only in the input-to-state transition. The result offers a more targeted architectural design grounded in the evaluated components' contributions.
neurips-2018-attention-in-convolutional-.tldr: Experiments on gesture recognition motivate an LSTM variant that keeps convolutions only in the input-to-state transition.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions when evaluating the objective function is expensive. Its decisions depend on a probabilistic model of that function, but choosing an appropriate model can itself be difficult. Limited observations make this choice especially consequential because gathering more evidence carries the same expense as the original optimization problem.

The paper introduces an automated approach that applies Bayesian optimization within the space of possible models. As observations arrive, it searches for promising explanations of the objective function. It also represents uncertainty about model selection: multiple models can contribute to the method's current beliefs and therefore influence subsequent decisions about where to evaluate the objective.

This connects model selection directly to the ongoing optimization process instead of treating it as a settled preliminary choice. The authors argue, and demonstrate empirically, that the approach finds suitable models and improves optimization efficiency. The stated finding concerns the benefit of adapting and combining models under uncertainty; it does not establish that one model is always best.
neurips-2018-automating-bayesian-optimiz.tldr: Bayesian optimization over model choices adapts the optimizer's beliefs and empirically improves the efficiency of optimizing expensive functions.

paragraphs: Related time series can contain common information without matching directly in their observed form. This paper develops a Bayesian model for recovering that shared information while allowing nonlinear alignment. Its motivating application is sensor data from wind turbines, where an underlying turbulent wind field introduces common structure across measurements.

The model allows transformations on both sides of the observation process. Input alignments account for how the series correspond, while flexible output transformations account for how observations are expressed. Together, these components form multiple deep Gaussian process models linked through hidden generating processes. This structure lets the model describe shared variation alongside the transformations needed to relate individual series.

The authors develop an efficient variational approximation using nested variational compression to make inference practical. They show how the resulting model extracts common information and separates the learning problem into interpretable functional components. Results on artificial data and measurements from two wind turbines illustrate this approach to understanding dependent time series with nonlinear differences.
neurips-2018-bayesian-alignments-of-warp.tldr: A Bayesian model jointly learns nonlinear time-series alignments and observation transformations to recover shared hidden structure.

paragraphs: Discovering cancer subtypes from sequencing data involves two linked challenges. The data are counts with substantial variability, and the number of patients can be small relative to the number of measured molecules and the complexity of disease. Combining information across sources could help, provided that differences between those sources are handled appropriately.

The paper proposes Bayesian Multi-Domain Learning, which uses hierarchical negative binomial factorization to model overdispersed counts. It learns hidden representations that depend on the domain, allowing the modeling framework to incorporate multiple sources while retaining domain-specific structure. The intended benefit is accurate cancer subtyping even when a particular cancer type has relatively few samples.

Experiments use both simulated data and sequencing datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas. The reported findings show promising potential for learning across domains without the harmful transfer effects observed in some existing methods. This supports the value of combining a count-appropriate model with domain-dependent representations, while keeping the evidence at the level of the tested datasets.
neurips-2018-bayesian-multi-domain-learn.tldr: A Bayesian model combines sequencing count data across domains to support cancer subtyping when samples for individual cancer types are limited.

paragraphs: Clustering uncertainty concerns the many possible ways a dataset could be divided into groups. Computing a full probability distribution over those possibilities is difficult because the number of partitions grows rapidly. This paper develops a compact representation and a dynamic-programming procedure for exact inference over clusterings.

The procedure computes three quantities exactly: the normalization needed for the distribution, the probability of an individual cluster, and the most probable complete clustering. Its time and space requirements scale with the set of subsets of the data rather than the much larger set of all partitions. It also improves the time complexity of an earlier algorithm by a factor equal to the number of data points.

The computation remains large, so the exact method is relevant particularly to small datasets. The authors also explore sparse approximations for greater scalability. Experiments on gene-expression data used in cancer treatment report advantages over approximate methods, illustrating why retaining clustering uncertainty exactly can matter in practical small-data applications.
neurips-2018-compact-representation-of-u.tldr: Dynamic programming makes exact clustering uncertainty calculations substantially smaller, enabling small-data applications and motivating scalable approximations.

paragraphs: Designing controls for fluid flow is challenging because the governing dynamics are nonlinear. Accurate computational fluid simulations offer a way to learn models that could support controller design. This paper studies that possibility for airflow around a cylinder, using simulation data as the basis for learning how the system changes over time.

The proposed method is grounded in Koopman theory and learns both forced and unforced dynamics. Covering both cases means addressing the flow's evolution with and without external forcing. The authors show that their learned dynamical models are stable and can predict the cylinder system over extended time horizons, making them useful for considering the future consequences of control actions.

They then use the learned models within model predictive control. For the studied cylinder system, this produces a straightforward and interpretable control law that suppresses vortex shedding in the wake. The contribution therefore links learned dynamics to a concrete control outcome, showing how simulation-based modeling can inform an understandable intervention in a nonlinear flow.
neurips-2018-deep-dynamical-modeling-and.tldr: Models learned from fluid simulations support long-horizon prediction and an interpretable control law for suppressing vortex shedding behind a cylinder.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can make strong predictions while remaining difficult to interpret. For scientific applications, explanations that are sensitive to noise also raise concerns about whether discoveries will be reproducible. This paper addresses that problem through feature selection: identifying relevant inputs while explicitly controlling errors in the selection process.

The proposed method, DeepPINK, combines a new neural-network architecture with the knockoffs framework. This integration lets the model perform nonlinear feature selection with a controlled error rate while maintaining high power, meaning an ability to identify relevant features. Error control and power serve complementary purposes: limiting mistaken selections and preserving useful discoveries.

The authors apply DeepPINK to simulated and real datasets to demonstrate its empirical utility. Its contribution is to connect neural-network interpretation with a statistical selection criterion, giving feature discoveries an explicit error-control objective. The stated results support this approach to interpretability and reproducibility through selected inputs, rather than claiming a complete explanation of every internal computation in a deep network.
neurips-2018-deeppink-reproducible-featu.tldr: DeepPINK combines a neural-network architecture with knockoffs to select features with controlled errors while maintaining high power.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test claims about a population proportion while satisfying differential privacy. It derives uniformly most powerful tests for simple and one-sided hypotheses, focusing on performance at finite sample sizes. Within the relevant privacy and testing constraints, the goal is to maximize the ability to detect alternatives.

The authors express privacy requirements for hypothesis tests as linear constraints. For exchangeable data, they show that tests can be expressed using the empirical distribution. They use this structure to establish a private counterpart of the Neyman-Pearson lemma for binomial observations, where the resulting optimal test depends only on the sample sum.

The tests can also be implemented by processing a random variable from a newly introduced distribution called Tulap. This representation provides easily computed exact p-values. The authors extend their results to distribution-free tests for continuous data, and simulations show exact type I error and higher power than existing techniques. These findings connect privacy constraints to concrete optimal testing procedures.
neurips-2018-differentially-private-unif.tldr: The paper derives optimal differentially private tests for specified binomial hypotheses, with exact p-values and finite-sample error control.

paragraphs: Natural images may occupy several separate regions of a data space rather than one connected region. This paper investigates what that possibility means for generative adversarial networks. It shows that single-generator GANs cannot correctly model a distribution supported on a disconnected manifold and studies the consequences for sample quality, missing modes, and local convergence.

The authors then examine how a collection of generators can address the disconnected structure. Multiple generators provide a way to represent separated parts of the distribution. However, the paper also identifies serious problems with fixing the prior over that collection, meaning fixing how the generators are weighted when producing samples.

The proposed approach learns that prior and infers the necessary number of generators without supervision. The authors describe the modifications as applicable on top of other GAN models. Experiments illustrate the original structural problem, its practical consequences, and the effectiveness of the modifications in alleviating it. The motivation remains conditional on data having disconnected support, which the abstract presents as a possibility for natural images.
neurips-2018-disconnected-manifold-learn.tldr: Learning a collection of generators and their weights helps GANs model distributions supported on disconnected regions.

paragraphs: In a partially observed strategy game, a player must act without seeing the complete game state. This paper frames defogging as two related tasks: estimating the current state and predicting future states from earlier incomplete observations. The aim is to turn the visible history into useful information about what remains hidden.

The authors propose encoder-decoder neural networks that combine convolutional and recurrent components. These components exploit spatial relationships and sequential patterns in a large dataset of human StarCraft: Brood War games. They also introduce proxy tasks and comparison methods to evaluate whether the networks capture basic game rules and broader game dynamics.

To test practical relevance, the authors use the learned models to predict enemy units inside an existing rule-based StarCraft bot. They observe improved win rates against several strong community bots. This connects the prediction task to actual game decisions: estimating unseen units can help an established decision system, with the reported benefit demonstrated against the opponents included in the evaluation.
neurips-2018-forward-modeling-for-partia.tldr: Neural models estimate hidden and future StarCraft states, improving a rule-based bot's win rates against several tested opponents.

paragraphs: Inverse optimization learns preferences and restrictions that could explain a decision maker's behavior. Its evidence consists of external signals paired with the decisions made in response. Many existing approaches assume that all such observations are available together, which limits their suitability for applications where decisions arrive continuously.

This paper proposes a general online-learning framework for inverse optimization. Its algorithm uses an implicit update rule and can handle noisy observations, allowing the inferred model to change as new evidence becomes available. This reformulates preference learning as an ongoing process rather than a calculation requiring the complete dataset in advance.

Under additional regularity assumptions on the data and model, the authors prove convergence at a rate of O(1/√T) and statistical consistency. These guarantees are conditional on those assumptions. Experiments report accurate parameter learning, strong robustness to noise, and a substantial computational improvement over batch learning. Together, the theory and experiments support online inverse optimization as an approach for learning from sequential decisions.
neurips-2018-generalized-inverse-optimiz.tldr: An online inverse-optimization algorithm learns from noisy decisions and has convergence and consistency guarantees under additional regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Learning representations can serve two different goals: separating categories so they are easy to recognize, and exposing the distinct factors that compose them. This paper combines these goals in a single embedding approach. It aims to support learning from few examples while encouraging representations whose components are more interpretable and independently useful.

The authors introduce a loss based on the F statistic, which measures separation among distributions. The key design is to separate classes on a subset of embedding dimensions without requiring separation everywhere. That leaves other dimensions available to express additional structure, encouraging disentanglement while retaining information useful for distinguishing classes.

In the reported evaluations, the method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance on recall@k and few-shot learning tasks. It also outperforms several alternatives on modularity and explicitness, the two evaluated properties of disentangled representations. These results support the proposed compatibility between useful class separation and disentanglement; the loss encourages that structure rather than establishing that every learned dimension must have a distinct meaning.
neurips-2018-learning-deep-disentangled-.tldr: An F-statistic loss separates classes on selected embedding dimensions, supporting few-shot learning while encouraging disentangled representations.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when all input vectors are known but responses must be requested individually. The objective is to query few responses and still obtain nearly the smallest possible squared loss across the entire dataset. Selecting diverse groups of points is particularly valuable when the response budget is very small.

Volume sampling produces an unbiased estimate of the optimal regression weights, but the authors show that it can perform poorly when a highly accurate loss approximation is required. They introduce a rescaled version that preserves unbiasedness while avoiding this behavior. With high probability, O(d log d + d/epsilon) responses suffice for loss within a factor of 1+epsilon of the minimum.

This improves the previously known O(d²/epsilon) sample requirement for an unbiased estimator. The rescaling also leads to an efficient volume-sampling algorithm based on determinantal rejection sampling. Supporting contributions include combinatorial results and bounds for dependent random matrices, connecting the response-efficiency guarantee to a concrete sampling procedure.
neurips-2018-leveraged-volume-sampling-f.tldr: Rescaled volume sampling preserves unbiased regression estimates while reducing the responses sufficient for a high-probability near-optimal loss guarantee.

paragraphs: Multilingual document collections can contain related themes expressed in different languages. Topic models help reveal those patterns, but slow processing and limited opportunities for user refinement can make them awkward for everyday exploration. This paper addresses both issues, including settings where information changes quickly and users need useful results promptly.

The authors first develop a multilingual anchoring algorithm that constructs an anchor-based topic model across languages. They then add interactive refinement through a system called MTAnchor. This gives users a role in shaping the topics the model produces, connecting automatic discovery with the needs of the person exploring the documents.

The algorithms are evaluated on labeled English, Chinese, and Sinhalese documents. The reported results show that interpretable topics useful for specific classification tasks can be produced within minutes. The contribution therefore combines multilingual modeling, speed, and user interaction. Its practical significance is that topic discovery becomes something users can refine during exploration, with usefulness demonstrated on the classification tasks studied.
neurips-2018-multilingual-anchoring-inte.tldr: MTAnchor lets users refine multilingual topic models that produce interpretable, task-useful topics within minutes in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Predicting when health events will occur becomes difficult when several outcomes are related. Some events affect few patients, and only a fraction of those events are observed in the data. A model must therefore account for competing risks while learning from strongly imbalanced evidence across outcome types.

This paper introduces a survival model that can use a shared representation of related events. Its procedure is sequential: survival distributions for individual outcomes become components of flexible multivariate estimators, which are then combined into an ensemble. The combination is designed to support accurate predictions across all outcome types simultaneously and correct for imbalance in observed outcomes.

The authors present the algorithm as the first boosting-like method for time-to-event data with multiple outcomes and demonstrate its performance on synthetic and real data. The central contribution is a way to combine outcome-specific predictions while sharing information among related events. That design directly addresses the difficulty of learning several correlated event distributions when evidence for individual outcomes is scarce.
neurips-2018-multitask-boosting-for-surv.tldr: A boosting-like survival model shares information across related outcomes and addresses imbalance when predicting competing time-to-event risks.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network can produce realistic individual samples while representing only a narrow part of the training distribution. This lack of diversity is called mode collapse. PacGAN addresses it by changing what the discriminator sees when deciding whether examples are real or generated.

The proposed technique, packing, presents multiple samples together, all drawn from the same class: either real data or generated data. The discriminator therefore makes a decision about a collection rather than an isolated example. This provides a way for the training signal to reflect distributional diversity across samples, which is central to the mode-collapse problem.

Using tools from binary hypothesis testing, including Blackwell's result, the authors prove a fundamental connection between packing and mode collapse. They show that packing penalizes generators exhibiting collapse and favors distributions with less collapse during training. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets suggest significant improvements. The theoretical and experimental claims support packing as a principled intervention, without asserting that it completely eliminates collapse in every GAN.
neurips-2018-pacgan-the-power-of-two-sam.tldr: PacGAN makes the discriminator judge groups of samples, creating a training penalty for mode collapse and suggesting significant empirical improvements.

paragraphs: Distributed training spreads a neural network's computational work across machines, but communication can affect how quickly training actually finishes. This paper focuses on elapsed training time in systems based on AllReduce operations. It examines the practical timing of distributed work rather than relying only on the appeal of a communication mechanism.

The authors develop timing models that include network latency, bandwidth, the number of machines, and computation time. These factors jointly determine the cost of coordinating training. Based on this analysis, they propose Pipe-SGD, a decentralized framework using pipelined training with a width of two, which they describe as combining benefits of synchronous and asynchronous approaches.

On a four-node GPU cluster, the reported wall-clock training improvement reaches up to 5.4 times compared with conventional approaches. That figure belongs to the evaluated setup and is an upper reported improvement. The broader contribution is to connect a particular pipeline design with an explicit account of the communication and computation costs that determine real training speed.
neurips-2018-pipe-sgd-a-decentralized-pi.tldr: Pipe-SGD uses a width-two training pipeline and reports up to 5.4-fold wall-clock speedups on a four-node GPU cluster.

paragraphs: Recovering an unknown vector from noisy linear measurements often requires knowledge of what plausible solutions look like. Plug-in methods incorporate that knowledge through a denoiser that can be designed separately from the measurement-handling procedure. Such methods have performed well, but obtaining rigorous predictions of their reconstruction error has been difficult.

This paper studies plug-in denoising within Vector Approximate Message Passing, or VAMP, an algorithm derived using Expectation Propagation techniques. The arrangement combines a structured estimation procedure with a modular denoising function. Its purpose is to retain flexibility in representing prior knowledge while making the resulting reconstruction performance mathematically analyzable.

The authors show that the mean squared error of plug-in VAMP can be predicted exactly for a large class of high-dimensional random measurement matrices and denoisers. The scope of that claim is the class covered by their analysis. Illustrations in image reconstruction and parametric bilinear estimation connect the theory to concrete estimation problems, addressing a gap between practical plug-in performance and rigorous error characterization.
neurips-2018-plug-in-estimation-in-high-.tldr: The paper rigorously predicts plug-in VAMP's mean squared error for a large class of high-dimensional random measurement matrices and denoisers.

paragraphs: Saliency maps highlight input features presented as relevant to a model's prediction. On images, a map can look convincing simply because it emphasizes recognizable structure. This paper argues that visual appeal alone is an unreliable way to judge whether the map explains what a trained model has learned.

The authors propose practical tests for assessing the kinds of explanations a saliency method can provide. Extensive experiments find that some methods are independent of both the model and the process generating the data. For methods that fail these tests, a persuasive-looking visualization does not establish that it reflects the learned relationship between inputs and outputs.

This matters for model debugging, outlier detection, and other tasks that require sensitivity to the model or data. The authors compare the behavior to image edge detection, which can reveal visual structure without using a trained model. Theory for a linear model and a single-layer convolutional network supports the experimental findings. The conclusion targets the methods that fail the tests, rather than rejecting every saliency approach.
neurips-2018-sanity-checks-for-saliency-.tldr: Some visually convincing saliency methods fail tests of model and data dependence, making them unsuitable for explanations that require those dependencies.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization seeks a compact structure underlying a data matrix, but outliers can distort the result. Using absolute-error loss often improves robustness over squared-error loss, yet even that approach can be insufficient. This paper proposes nonconvex losses to improve robustness while also addressing the computational cost of fitting the model.

The harder optimization problem is handled through majorization-minimization, which uses a surrogate objective to guide updates. The authors introduce a new surrogate and optimize its dual using an accelerated proximal gradient algorithm. This design exploits sparsity in the data, addressing a shortcoming of the existing robust factorization solver discussed in the paper.

The resulting algorithm has low time and space requirements and is guaranteed to converge to a critical point. That guarantee concerns a critical point, not necessarily the globally best solution. Extensive experiments report improvements over the state of the art in both accuracy and scalability. The contribution combines a more robust objective with an optimization procedure designed to make that objective computationally useful.
neurips-2018-scalable-robust-matrix-fact.tldr: A sparsity-aware optimization method makes nonconvex robust matrix factorization scalable and guarantees convergence to a critical point.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations can cause neural networks to fail even when the modified input appears nearly unchanged. Certified defenses seek mathematical guarantees covering every attacker within a specified family. One route is to upper-bound the worst possible loss, so the guarantee depends on how accurately that bound captures the network's behavior.

This paper introduces a semidefinite relaxation for certifying robustness of arbitrary ReLU networks. A relaxation makes the certification problem more tractable while bounding the original worst case. The authors show that their relaxation is tighter than previous alternatives, addressing loose bounds that can make otherwise relevant certificates uninformative.

A central result is that the method produces meaningful guarantees on three networks whose training objectives were not designed around this relaxation. This matters because earlier relaxations can be loose when applied to networks trained without them. The guarantees still concern the specified attacker family; applicability to arbitrary ReLU networks does not mean that every such network is robust or will receive a strong certificate.
neurips-2018-semidefinite-relaxations-fo.tldr: A tighter semidefinite relaxation provides meaningful robustness certificates for three ReLU networks trained without using that relaxation.

paragraphs: A neural network must learn representations that remain useful beyond its training examples. Regularization helps pursue that goal, but directly constraining hidden representations is less straightforward than penalizing parameter sizes. This paper analyzes supervised autoencoders, which jointly predict the desired targets and reconstruct their inputs.

The reconstruction objective provides an additional requirement for the learned representation: it must retain information useful for recovering the input as well as predicting the target. For linear autoencoders, the authors prove a generalization result through uniform stability arising from reconstruction error. Their analysis establishes an improvement over simpler norm regularization and more advanced regularization through auxiliary tasks.

The empirical study covers architectures with different hidden-unit counts and activation functions. Across those evaluated settings, adding the supervised autoencoder objective never harms performance relative to the corresponding standard network and can significantly improve generalization. This finding is empirical for the tested architectures, while the stated theoretical guarantee is for linear autoencoders. Together, they provide complementary reasons to consider reconstruction as a regularizer.
neurips-2018-supervised-autoencoders-imp.tldr: Joint input reconstruction and target prediction improve generalization in the reported experiments, with a supporting stability result for linear autoencoders.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms help a model emphasize relevant features and can be used to interpret its predictions. However, the networks producing attention are often only weakly supervised, so their apparent emphasis may be unreliable. This paper introduces uncertainty into attention itself, allowing an explanation to express how confidently the model assigns importance.

The proposed Uncertainty-aware Attention mechanism generates feature attention with input-dependent noise. It learns larger variance for instances about which it is uncertain, and the authors train it using variational inference. The result associates attention with both a learned emphasis and a measure of variability, providing more information than attention values alone.

On risk-prediction tasks using electronic health records, the model significantly outperforms existing attention models. Analysis finds attention patterns consistent with clinicians' interpretations and richer explanations through the learned variance. Further evaluations examine uncertainty calibration and prediction when the model can decline to decide. These results support the reported reliability of the approach across prediction, interpretation, and uncertainty assessment in the studied tasks.
neurips-2018-uncertainty-aware-attention.tldr: Input-dependent uncertainty in attention improves clinical risk prediction and adds information about the reliability of feature emphasis.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering can produce highly unbalanced groups in sparse, random graphs. This paper explains that behavior through small tree-like sets attached to the main graph by a single edge. Graph conductance is sensitive to these weakly connected sets, and spectral clustering inherits that sensitivity, potentially treating peripheral noise as meaningful structure.

The authors analyze an existing regularization method by relating it to conductance on a modified graph. They call this criterion CoreCut and show that minimizing it relaxes to regularized spectral clustering. Examining CoreCut reveals why the regularized procedure is less sensitive to dangling sets, connecting the algorithmic modification to a concrete change in the partitioning objective.

The resulting explanation interprets unbalanced partitions as overfitting to noise at the graph's periphery and shows how regularization corrects that behavior. The analysis also demonstrates how regularization can improve computational speed. Simulations and data examples illustrate both aspects, giving a structural account of why regularization can improve clustering quality and computation in the studied setting.
neurips-2018-understanding-regularized-s.tldr: A conductance-based analysis explains how regularization reduces spectral clustering's sensitivity to noisy peripheral sets and can improve speed.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian inference seeks a manageable representation of a probability distribution that is difficult to work with directly. This paper introduces Wasserstein variational inference, an approach grounded in optimal transport. It uses a new family of divergences that contains both f-divergences and Wasserstein distance as special cases.

The method obtains gradients of its variational objective by backpropagating through Sinkhorn iterations. This connects the transport-based comparison of distributions to a trainable optimization procedure. The authors report a very stable likelihood-free training method that can work with implicit distributions and probabilistic programs, making the framework relevant when training does not rely on evaluating a likelihood.

The authors also use the framework to introduce several new autoencoder forms and evaluate their robustness and performance against existing variational autoencoding techniques. These applications show how the inference construction can lead to concrete representation-learning models. The abstract reports the stability of the training method and the comparative evaluation, without claiming that every proposed autoencoder outperforms the existing alternatives.
neurips-2018-wasserstein-variational-inf.tldr: Wasserstein variational inference uses optimal-transport divergences and differentiable Sinkhorn iterations for stable likelihood-free Bayesian approximation.
